name: not-pair?
summary: True when the object is anything other than a pair -- the exact negation of pair?.
explanation: not-pair? is (lambda (x) (not (pair? x))) given a name, and the reason SRFI-1 bothers to name it is that the negation is what you actually pass around. A recursive walk over a tree stops at the leaves, and a leaf is precisely a non-pair; a flattener asks the same question; so does anything deciding whether it has reached the bottom of a nested structure. Written inline as (not (pair? x)) that test is a lambda you have to build every time, and it reads as the absence of a thing rather than the presence of one. Named, it becomes a first-class predicate you can hand to any, every, filter, or partition directly. The verb adds no power. It adds a name for the stopping condition of every structural recursion over lists, which is a concept worth being able to point at.

examples.note: (#f #t #t #t #f) -- only the two pairs answer #f, and the empty list is not a pair.
(leaves (1 sym ()) pairs ((2 3) (a . b))) -- as a predicate it partitions a mixed list without a lambda.

examples.code:
(define (depth x)
  (if (not-pair? x) 0 (+ 1 (apply max (map depth (list (car x) (cdr x)))))))
(display (map depth (list 'atom '(1) '(1 (2 (3))) (cons (cons 1 2) 3))))
(newline)
examples.note: (0 2 5 2) -- not-pair? is the base case, and the whole recursion is one line because the stopping test has a name.

caveats: The empty list is NOT a pair, so (not-pair? '()) is #t. If you are walking a proper list, null? is the test you want, not this one.
It says nothing about lists. A dotted pair (a . b) answers #f just as (a b c) does, because both are pairs.
It is the negation of pair?, not of list?. (not-pair? '(1 2 . 3)) is #f even though that is not a proper list.
Strings and vectors are not pairs. A recursion that uses not-pair? as its leaf test will treat a vector as a leaf and never descend into it.
Anything that is not a pair is a leaf by this test, including procedures and the unspecified value. That is usually what you want in a tree walk, and occasionally exactly not.
usecases: The base case of any structural recursion over cons trees -- flatten, depth, tree-map, leaf-count.
Partitioning a heterogeneous list into atoms and sublists without writing a lambda.
Guarding a car or cdr: if not-pair? holds, the accessor would raise.

learn.concept: Naming the negation makes the stopping condition of a recursion into something you can pass around.
learn.progression: Write flatten with (not (pair? x)) inline. Then write depth, and leaf-count, and tree-map, and notice you wrote the same lambda four times. Then discover not-pair? and understand that SRFI-1 named it for exactly that reason.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (flatten-tree t)
  (cond ((null? t) '())
        ((not-pair? t) (list t))
        (else (append (flatten-tree (car t)) (flatten-tree (cdr t))))))
(display (list 'nested (flatten-tree '(1 (2 (3 4)) 5))
               'flat (flatten-tree '(a b c))
               'atom (flatten-tree 'lone)))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A serializer must walk an arbitrary cons tree and emit every leaf. Candidates: not-pair? (one named predicate, correct for dotted structure, and directly passable to filter), (not (pair? x)) inline (identical behavior, but rebuilt at every call site and unusable as an argument), null? (wrong -- it stops only at the empty list and blows up on an atom in the cdr position), list? (wrong and expensive -- it walks the whole spine at every node, turning a linear walk quadratic), atom? (not bound in Motoi at all; it is a Lisp name, not a Scheme one). not-pair? is the pick because a leaf is defined by the absence of structure, and that is the thing being tested.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: a flattener whose leaf test is not-pair?, run on a nested list, a flat one, and a bare atom that is not a list at all. math: counting leaves in three trees including a dotted pair, where the count is 2 because both car and cdr are leaves. cs: tallying atoms against cells across an all-atom list, an all-pair list, and a mixed one containing the empty list, which counts as an atom.
row-2-audit.meta: The dotted pair (cons 1 2) is in every one of these on purpose. It is the case where null?-based recursion breaks and not-pair?-based recursion does not, and it is the reason the two predicates are not interchangeable.
row-2-audit.eng: A flattener that recurses on car and cdr separately handles improper structure for free. One that recurses on cdr while assuming a proper list does not.
row-2-audit.math: Leaf count over a binary cons tree satisfies L(leaf) = 1 and L(node) = L(car) + L(cdr). The empty list is a leaf under this definition, which is why '(1 2) has three leaves and not two.
row-2-audit.cs: Using list? as a leaf test costs a spine walk per node and turns an O(n) traversal into O(n^2). pair? is O(1) and so is its negation.

row-3-dimension.setup: Deciding whether you have hit the bottom of a structure and should stop descending.

rungs.domain: a bill of materials where a part is either a raw item or an assembly of sub-parts
rungs.code:
(define bom '(chassis (wheel bolt bolt) (seat (frame) cushion)))
(define (raw-parts x)
  (cond ((null? x) '())
        ((not-pair? x) (list x))
        (else (append (raw-parts (car x)) (raw-parts (cdr x))))))
(define (assembly-count x)
  (cond ((null? x) 0)
        ((not-pair? x) 0)
        ((not-pair? (car x)) (assembly-count (cdr x)))
        (else (+ 1 (assembly-count (car x)) (assembly-count (cdr x))))))
(display (list 'raw (raw-parts bom) 'assemblies (assembly-count bom)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a rewriter substituting variables throughout a symbolic expression
rungs.code:
(define (substitute expr from to)
  (cond ((not-pair? expr) (if (eq? expr from) to expr))
        (else (cons (substitute (car expr) from to)
                    (substitute (cdr expr) from to)))))
(define e '(+ (* x 2) (- x y)))
(display (list 'once (substitute e 'x 9)
               'chained (substitute (substitute e 'x 'u) 'y 'u)))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare values it is a four-way classification and nothing more. On a bill of materials the same predicate is doing two different jobs in the same walk -- collecting leaves in one function, and in the other testing the CAR to decide whether a node is an assembly or just a labelled list, which is a different question asked with the same verb. In the rewriter the predicate is no longer selecting what to collect but what to TRANSFORM: leaves get compared and possibly replaced, nodes get rebuilt, and the recursion returns a tree of the same shape rather than a flat list or a number. Same one-argument test; it goes from classifier, to structural discriminator, to the branch point of a total function on trees.
row-3-dimension.meta: The three rungs return three different kinds of thing: a boolean, a list and a count, and a rebuilt tree. That is deliberate -- not-pair? is the branch, and what changes up the ladder is what each branch is allowed to produce.
row-3-dimension.eng: A bill of materials is a tree where the leaves are the things you actually buy. Explosion is a leaf collection, and sub-assembly counting is a node count over the same walk.
row-3-dimension.math: Substitution over a term algebra is defined by cases on constructors: atoms map through a function, applications map componentwise. not-pair? is that case split.
row-3-dimension.cs: Rebuilding with cons rather than list preserves improper tails, so the rewriter is total over all cons structure instead of only over proper lists.

row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (exactly-one-side? x)
  (let ((p (pair? x)) (n (not-pair? x)))
    (and (or p n) (not (and p n)))))
(display (map exactly-one-side? (list '() '(1 . 2) 0 #f (cons '() '()) (vector 1))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (safe-to-take-car? x) (if (not-pair? x) #t (pair? x)))
(define (leaf-recursion-terminates? t)
  (let count ((x t) (fuel 200))
    (cond ((= fuel 0) #f)
          ((not-pair? x) #t)
          (else (and (count (car x) (- fuel 1)) (count (cdr x) (- fuel 1)))))))
(display (list 'guard (map safe-to-take-car? (list 1 '() '(1 2) (cons 1 2)))
               'halts (map leaf-recursion-terminates?
                           (list 'a '(1 2 3) '((1 (2)) . 3) '()))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: not-pair? agrees with the negation of pair? on every object without exception; pair? and not-pair? partition the universe so that exactly one of them holds; and because the empty list answers #t, a recursion using not-pair? as its base case terminates on every finite cons structure including improper ones.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all objects x, not-pair?(x) = not(pair?(x)); exactly one of pair?(x) and not-pair?(x) is true; and the structural recursion that stops at not-pair? reaches a leaf along every path of any finite cons tree
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims: agreement, exhaustive partition, and termination. What would falsify them: an object where the two predicates disagreed, one where both or neither held, or a structure where the recursion ran past the fuel because some non-pair failed to be recognised as a leaf. The empty list and the dotted pair appear in all three because they are the two shapes where the naive test null? would have given a different -- and wrong -- answer.
row-4-proof.eng: The agreement law is what lets you rewrite (not (pair? x)) to not-pair? mechanically across a codebase with no review.
row-4-proof.math: A two-valued predicate and its negation partition the domain. The proof of a partition is that the disjunction holds and the conjunction does not, which is what the middle program checks pointwise.
row-4-proof.cs: Termination is the practical payoff. Because every non-pair is a leaf, no cons tree has a path that avoids the base case -- which is exactly the guarantee null? does not give you.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (leaf? x) (not-pair? x))
(define (tree-map f t)
  (if (leaf? t) (f t) (cons (tree-map f (car t)) (tree-map f (cdr t)))))
(display (list 'doubled (tree-map (lambda (x) (if (number? x) (* 2 x) x)) '(1 (2 3) 4))
               'dotted (tree-map (lambda (x) (if (number? x) (+ x 100) x)) (cons 1 2))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (atom? x) (not-pair? x))
(define (tree-fold f seed t)
  (if (atom? t) (f t seed) (tree-fold f (tree-fold f seed (cdr t)) (car t))))
(define (sum-numbers t) (tree-fold (lambda (x acc) (if (number? x) (+ x acc) acc)) 0 t))
(display (map sum-numbers (list '(1 2 3) '(1 (2 (3 (4)))) '(a (b 5) c) (cons 7 8))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (terminal? x) (not-pair? x))
(define (paths t)
  (if (terminal? t)
      (list (list t))
      (append (map (lambda (p) (cons 'a p)) (paths (car t)))
              (map (lambda (p) (cons 'd p)) (paths (cdr t))))))
(display (list 'small (paths (cons 1 2))
               'count (length (paths '(1 (2 3))))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: not-pair? answers whether an object has no cons structure to descend into.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: leaf? is one call; tree-map is built on it and rebuilds any cons structure with its leaves transformed, which works on improper trees because the base case is defined by absence of structure rather than by reaching the empty list. math: atom? is one call; tree-fold reduces an entire tree to a single value, and sum-numbers is then one line -- the fold does the walking and the caller only says what to do with a leaf. cs: terminal? is one call; paths enumerates every route from root to leaf as a sequence of car and cdr steps, which is a complete structural description of the tree derived from nothing but the stopping test.
row-5-emergence.meta: All three helpers are one-line aliases, and that is the point -- the emergent power is not in the wrapper but in the fact that a NAMED stopping condition lets tree-map, tree-fold, and paths all be four lines. Every one of them calls its helper on every node, so removing the alias would break all three.
row-5-emergence.eng: tree-map over arbitrary cons structure is the generic form of map. It is the same shape as map on lists once you stop assuming the cdr is a list.
row-5-emergence.math: A fold over a tree is a catamorphism: the leaf case supplies the algebra, the node case supplies the recursion. Everything else is a choice of f.
row-5-emergence.cs: Path enumeration is how you index into a tree without an ordering. The number of paths is the number of leaves, which recovers leaf-count as a corollary rather than a second traversal.
